question: An operations analyst has a Claude-generated list of two thousand customer accounts that supposedly meet the company's dormancy rule and are due to be closed. Closing an account cannot be reversed. What should the analyst do first?
options: A) Proceed with the closures, because the dormancy rule the list was built from is the company's own written rule.
B) Ask Claude to go over its own list a second time and drop any account it is no longer confident belongs there.
C) Close the smallest accounts on the list first, so that any mistake would affect the least valuable customers.
D) Check a sample of the listed accounts against the source records to confirm the rule was applied correctly.
correct_answers: D) Check a sample of the listed accounts against the source records to confirm the rule was applied correctly.
explanations: A sound rule does not guarantee sound application of it. The question is whether this list correctly reflects the rule, and that has not been checked.
Asking the model to re-examine its own output gives no independent evidence. The list can only be validated against the source records it was supposedly derived from.
Sequencing by account value does not verify anything; it only rations the damage. Wrongly closing a small customer's account is still an irreversible error affecting a real person.

Correct. The action is irreversible and affects real customers, so verification has to happen before anything is executed. Sampling the list against the underlying records tests whether the rule was actually applied as intended, which is the one thing that cannot be fixed afterwards.
